planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in humus-rich, lime-free, constantly moist soil in deep shade; this fern grows slowly and resents both lime and drying out, so a cool, sheltered woodland or streamside position is essential for it to settle in.

directions: Hay-scented buckler fern is native to the cool, humid Atlantic coastlands of western Europe and the Macaronesian islands, where it carpets shaded, mossy rock slopes and stream banks that stay permanently damp. Its finely cut, triangular, tripinnate fronds have a crisped, almost crimped texture and a dark purplish-brown rachis dotted with reddish-brown scales, and the foliage releases a sweet, hay-like fragrance reminiscent of coumarin when it is cut or dried. Because it comes from a mild, oceanic climate, it performs best in consistently cool, lime-free, humus-rich soil in deep shade and is slow to bulk up, so established clumps should be disturbed as little as possible. It is an excellent choice for a shaded rock garden, streamside planting, or woodland trough where its delicate, lacy texture can be appreciated up close.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this wood fern tolerates heavier, damper ground than most Dryopteris species and is well suited to low spots and stream edges in a woodland garden.

directions: Caucasian wood fern grows naturally in the mixed and deciduous mountain forests between the Black and Caspian Seas, spanning the Caucasus, northeastern Turkey, and northwestern Iran. It forms a graceful, vase-shaped clump of arching, finely divided, deciduous fronds that give it a soft, lacy texture distinct from the coarser look of many other wood ferns. Unlike several of its relatives, it tolerates consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil without declining, making it a good candidate for the damper edges of a shade border or a spot near a downspout or pond margin. Give it partial to full shade and steady moisture and it will form a long-lived, trouble-free clump that needs little attention beyond an occasional spring tidy of old fronds.

planting.note: Tuck divisions or small container plants into moist, humus-rich pockets between rocks in partial to full shade in spring; this diminutive fern naturally roots at its frond tips, so allow room for new plantlets to establish along the crevice or rock face where it is planted.

directions: Jumping holly fern is a tiny, evergreen rock-dwelling species native to mountain forests of China, Japan, Korea, and the Russian Far East, where it colonizes damp, shaded rock slopes and crevices in small mats. Its narrow, once-pinnate fronds taper to a proliferous tip that roots wherever it touches moist ground, allowing a single plant to gradually produce a chain of new plantlets across a rock face or crevice, which gives rise to its common name. At only a few inches tall, it is best suited to a shaded rock garden, trough, or crevice planting where its small scale and colony-forming habit can be appreciated up close rather than lost among larger woodland ferns. Keep the planting pocket consistently moist but sharply drained, since it naturally grows where water moves through rock rather than standing.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this selection shares the species' tolerance for dry shade and neglect once its crown is established.

directions: 'Linearis' is an old male fern selection grown for fronds whose pinnae are narrowed and more widely spaced than the species, giving the whole frond an airier, more open look without the multi-forked, crested pinnae tips seen in 'Linearis Polydactyla'. It reaches the same substantial size as the wild species, forming a large, vase-shaped clump of semi-evergreen fronds that hold up well through a typical shade garden season. Like other male fern selections, it is unusually tolerant of dry shade, root competition, and general neglect once its crown is established, making it a dependable choice for difficult spots under trees. Divide congested clumps in spring every several years to maintain the open, narrow-pinnae character that distinguishes this form.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun with ample moisture in spring; its compact size makes it equally at home in a rock garden pocket or the front of a shaded border.

directions: 'Crispa', also offered as 'Crispatissima', is a compact dwarf form of male fern only a fraction the size of the species, with glossy mid- to bright-green fronds whose pinnae are crimped and ruffled along the edges for a distinctly textured, crinkled appearance. Its small, tidy, clump-forming habit suits the front of a shaded border, a rock garden pocket, or a mixed container in a way the larger wild species cannot. It tolerates dry shade once established but looks its best, and holds its crimped texture most cleanly, with regular moisture and a humus-rich soil. Mulch lightly each spring and remove tattered fronds before new fiddleheads unfurl to keep the compact rosette looking fresh.
